title: Monopoly Round-Up: Microsoft, the FAA, and Our Soviet Indifference to System Collapse.
author: Lee Hepner
content:
Welcome to the monopoly round-up. Lots of news, as usual. Nvidia CEO Jensen
Huang's downfall is the most important story of the week, by far, and we're
going to have a piece on that soon, taking a step back from the gossipy
parlour intrigue and reframing this event in terms of the political and policy
debates it is causing.

There was a lot of other important news this week, too, including a case to
block a veterinary services merger that would affect every pet lover in the
country, and some consequential leadership battles that could affect whether
the new Congress tackles corporate power, as Senator Chris Van Hollen launches
a bid to challenge Senator Schumer's leadership.

But first, I want to discuss two major outages of key infrastructure that
happened this week, the Microsoft Outlook collapse that caused a nationwide
work stoppage on Thursday, followed the next day by the nationwide ground stop
that prevented some 12,000 flights from taking off during a four hour period
on Friday. As of this writing, thousands of flights are still being canceled,
and stranded passengers are struggling to make it to their destinations.

### When Will We Stop Tolerating the Inevitability of Failure?

The Microsoft and air traffic control outages hit like a one-two punch last
week. And their scale was significant, because each of these systems are
infrastructure for their respective clients and industries. Microsoft Outlook
and the company's suite of office products are staples of modern work, the
technological infrastructure of government agencies, schools, for-profit and
nonprofit corporations, the largest law firms in the country, and more. As of
November 2026, there are about 450 million paid commercial subscribers to
Office 365, and another 95 million paid consumer licenses.

A significant portion of those subscribers, over a half billion of them in
total, saw their functions ground to a halt. One estimate put the cost of the
outage, which lasted from 21-24 hours for various services, at [$7
billion](https://please.untaint.us/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cnn.com%2F2026%2F11%2F12%2Fbusiness%2Flive-
news%2Fmicrosoft-global-outage-intl-hnk%3Ft%3D1794588874265%26post-
id%3Dcmwf6e7el00003b6txhzlcvvg&post-id=cmwf6e7el00003b6txhzlcvvg).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jvEP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae7171c8-757f-460f-8e50-6258a0510e49_1168x784.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jvEP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae7171c8-757f-460f-8e50-6258a0510e49_1168x784.jpeg)

In this case, it was the failure of a single component of an automated health
check that shut down one server, which redistributed that server's traffic to
other servers, which caused _those_ servers to become overloaded and shut
down, and so on and so on. Tech outages are not new or even rare, but the
scale of interconnectedness and dependency means that the extent of harm
caused by one missing puzzle piece is immense. It is a bit like we are in a
giant bank run, except with industrial and technical systems.

Around 10 hours into the Microsoft outage, which became widespread around
midday eastern time on Thursday, more than one group text I'm on had begun
discussing what it would mean if Outlook just… never came back? That thought
exercise is less about Outlook, our lives and work (inevitably) would
continue, but about the possibility that every other system we rely on could
be next.

Those discussions had hardly subsided when news broke that Federal Aviation
Administration issued its ominous Friday the 13th
[order](https://www.fly.faa.gov/ois/oisedit/adv_oisedit_dis?day=11132026&number=111&utm_source=chatgpt.com):

> DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY.  
> ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION  
> COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED.

For air traffic control, it was a failed router following a copper-to-fiber
migration that triggered the flooding of other routers, imperiling radar and
telecommunications systems. (Again, these are the current diagnoses, which may
change as more information comes out.)

The Microsoft and air traffic control outages happened back to back and
affected tens of millions of people across the country, so naturally there was
speculation that the incidents were somehow related, that the United States
had been the target of a ransomware or state-sponsored cyber attack, or that
we were witnessing the early onset of broader societal disruption. The verdict
may still be out on some of that.

### Cascading Failures

As a technical matter, both the Microsoft Outlook outage and the FAA's
nationwide ground stop were attributed to "**cascading failures** " following
technological upgrades. I like that term because it captures the domino-like
phenomenon where a single glitch in the system can quickly spiral into an
incapacitating social and economic crisis.

Cascading failures are what occur when systems are based on flawed and deeply
interdependent technologies. The quintessential example is Chernobyl, where
flawed systems and a culture of inadequate safety protocols created a hair
trigger for one error to cause a disaster.

In his 1984 book "[Normal
Accidents](https://maritimesafetyinnovationlab.org/wp-
content/uploads/2021/04/Normal-Accidents-Living-With-High-Risk-Technologies-
Perrow.pdf): Living With High-Risk Technologies," Charles Perrow introduced
the idea that certain systems are so complex and so tightly interwoven that
accidents are not merely possible, but inevitable. "Tightly-coupled" system
design was how we got Three Mile Island, and even in 1984, Perrow saw how we
were replicating high risk system design in the airline, maritime and space
industries, with weaponry and medicine, and dams and mining. The obvious
response is to create more resilience in our industrial infrastructure, to
lessen the likelihood of such incidents and reduce the damage when they occur.

Despite Perrow's diagnosis over 40 years ago, similar "interactive
complexities" have become even more prevalent in the networked era of the last
quarter century. It used to be that when you were having a tech problem, work
would call in the IT guy to resolve some local server issue. Now we've
constructed bespoke systems on top of remote servers and cloud-based
infrastructure that are, predictably, concentrated choke points for systemic
failure. Most businesses now outsource control over their own systems to large
firms.

Indeed, our political economy architecture over the past forty five years
encourages this kind of irresponsibility. First, there is a lack of liability
for firms like Microsoft when they cause damage. Second, labor law doesn't
protect the engineers who know how to protect these systems. One clear root
cause of cascading failures -- the first domino of system collapse, which
predates either of these incidents in isolation -- is getting rid of workers
who know best how to monitor for and mitigate risks.

Microsoft has laid off approximately 35,000 employees since October 2022, and
in May 2025 [laid off](https://www.reuters.com/business/world-at-
work/microsoft-lay-off-3-workforce-cnbc-reports-2025-05-13/) 3% of its entire
workforce, disproportionately software engineers, while beefing up project
management. Basically, the trend is toward replacing engineers, who understand
the importance of reinforcing weaknesses in the foundation, with a bunch of
well-paid efficiency hawks with a bias toward cutting corners on the path to
rapid product delivery.

Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says that up to 30% of the company's
code is now written by software. That percentage is much higher at other
companies, including Anthropic. Tech executives have
[recognized](https://diginomica.com/ai-now-touches-three-quarters-enterprise-
code-new-relics-ashan-willy-agent-debt-and-re-defining) the risk associated
with smaller teams having to scrutinize millions of lines of code they didn't
write, and products being shipped by managers who haven't had time to review
at all.

Another cause is weak antitrust law, which facilitates the creation of
chokepoints. As BIG asked
[years](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/counterfeit-capitalism-why-a-
monopolized) ago in explaining the shortages during the post-Covid era, "What
else is a monopoly but a business model designed to secure or create a
bottleneck?"

> It wasn't necessarily done in bad faith; policymakers followed the lead of
> economists, who believed dominant firms were dominant because they were
> efficient. This faith in efficiency over all else meant that the public
> structuring of markets to force resiliency - aka regulation - was
> illegitimate. Alas, this philosophy has led to a series of bottlenecks in
> our supply chains, which are now global.

I wish we had learned from the post-Covid era, but it's clear that we have
still not re-architected key social infrastructure to become more resilient.
Since 2021, it has gotten worse, with AI and cloud computing facilitating more
centralization. Here's investor Roger McNamee making that point:

### Can Companies Manage Their Own Systems?

Five hours into its outage, Microsoft issued an optimistic update: "We're
returning a portion of affected servers to the service, and they remain stable
so far," but followed it one hour later with, "The servers we returned to
service can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic."

These opaque updates and subsequent partisan finger-pointing suggested no one
really knew what was going on. Microsoft itself explained to investors the
nature of the problem. Highly interdependent systems magnify reliability
issues, it said, while admitting that they are rolling out technology without
adequate processes to detect defects:

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xBAt!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F494ab4a2-b6b2-4469-9de1-580a101773d1_1125x171.png)

According to Microsoft's July 2026 SEC [10-K
filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000119312526323660/msft-20260630.htm),
interdependencies magnify reliability issues, and pre-release defects may be
undetectable.

There will be studies, the obligatory reports and investigations, but even if
we arrive at some official technological consensus, the overriding perception
is that the most important and dominant corporations in our society are
deploying critical infrastructure without really knowing how it works.

Here's another example, from Anthropic's pre-IPO filing, which plainly states
their models are developing at such a rate they may soon become incapable of
monitoring for harmful conduct and misalignment:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ycSr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd499fbe4-4d93-4466-a7e6-1573d4341aa3_1003x274.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ycSr!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd499fbe4-4d93-4466-a7e6-1573d4341aa3_1003x274.png)In
Anthopic's pre-IPO S-1, they admit that "we may deploy models whose behavior
we cannot adequately verify." Is this okay?

When you bet the entire house on technology that even its makers admit is
unreliable, unsafe, and impervious to risk mitigation, and then something goes
wrong, an outside observer might fairly ask, "What did you expect?"

But the problem isn't isolated to private large corporations. We have ripped
out the capacity of public institutions as well. Earlier this year, the FAA
reduced its [target number](https://www.reuters.com/business/world-at-
work/faa-cuts-target-air-traffic-control-staffing-2026-05-15) of air traffic
controllers by 2,000 personnel, even though since 2015 the amount of air
traffic has increased by 10% and the number of controllers has declined by 6%.
Many controllers now work six day weeks with compulsory overtime. Nearly
11,000 air traffic controllers are still due months of back pay for a 2.8%
raise granted by Congress, which the FAA refuses to pay.

Air traffic controllers are understaffed, overworked, and underpaid. We know
this, yet are moving in the direction of making that problem worse. That's the
broader context in which the FAA announced, just three days prior to the
outage, the nationwide rollout of its AI-assisted SMART system -- despite
concerns from Congress as to its safety and over the objections of air traffic
control unions. I'm sure the timing is just a coincidence, nothing to see
here, move right along, right? Or maybe, just maybe, it's worth asking once
again, _**What did you expect?**_

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nRg2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F60229c88-30e7-4c26-bfb8-66d601fbe176_1425x420.png)

Broad systemic failures are avoidable, yet we've made them inevitable. It's
hard to imagine that changing any time soon, because we can't expect to govern
when we have given up on understanding how things work. And while this time
it's "just" Outlook, or "just" an annoyance isolated to people with the
misfortune of having to travel this weekend, sometime soon it will be a much
larger problem. The parallels to Chernobyl aren't just theoretical. Nuclear
power plants use Outlook, too.

There's also just the _Microsoft_ of it all. Microsoft is one of the enduring
monopolies of the past 50 years, ever since it acquired the operating system
called DOS in 1981 and wielded it to achieve monopoly control over personal
computers. There's a colloquial wisdom that Microsoft's power has waned amid
competition with the likes of Google and Apple, but it's more accurate to say
that Microsoft has burrowed itself into core markets -- like enterprise
communications software -- through sticky procurement contracts that produce
[moral hazards](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.07766v2) through vendor lock-in.

If Microsoft's refusal to improve the basic search indexing function of
Outlook is a reflection of its insulation from competitive pressure, which it
clearly is, then this week's outage is even less surprising as a function of
the lack of competitive pressure it faces to make its systems resilient.

The larger question here is whether policymakers have over-indexed on
optimizing the efficiency of individual systems, which increases the
vulnerability of larger, interdependent systems. That's the way to think about
cascading failures. It's a critical concern not just for work emails and
aviation, but for financial markets, telecommunications, energy, healthcare,
and cloud computing.

One big lesson of the pandemic was single points of failure in supply chains
were dangerous. They resulted in nationwide shortages of [baby
formula](https://www.economicliberties.us/our-work/the-guardian-the-us-baby-
formula-shortage-isnt-bad-luck-it-was-completely-preventable/), medical
[contrast dye](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/contrast-dye-shortage-
covid-19-pandemic-china-2022/) used in CT scans, and
[semiconductors](https://www.appliedenergysystems.com/semiconductor-shortages-
effect-on-auto-industry/) used in automobile manufacturing. A society that
prioritizes efficiency and scale, at the expense of resiliency and redundancy,
is doomed to the inevitable stream of shortages, outages, and eventually even
greater system collapse. In other words, we are going to restructure our
corporate systems, it's just a question of whether we do it deliberately,
hiring the necessary people to manage the risk, or whether we do it after a
collapse has harmed a lot more people.

Or to put it differently, we'll know America is on the right path when
Microsoft makes Outlook search actually work.

Now, on to the Good and Bad news of the week. Democrats are organizing around
an agenda for the new Congress, one which centers economic populism, but not
if leadership can't create the pathways to govern. A shakeup is coming for the
FTC, the Fox acquisition of Roku appears tainted by corruption, Chuck Schumer
is facing a real challenge for Senate leadership, and much more below.
